units.L3.1: Names and epithets: Li Taibai, Qinglian Jushi, Zhexianren, Shixian, Li Hanlin
units.L5.1: Era: Tang dynasty (701–762; alternative birth and death dates also exist)
units.L6.1: Birthplace: one account places his birth in Suyab, near modern Tokmok in Kyrgyzstan, and his family's move to Changlong in Mianzhou, near modern Jiangyou in Sichuan, when he was about five; another places his birth in Shu
units.L7.1: Identity: poet, former Hanlin attendant, and widely travelled man of letters
units.L8.1: Overview: a Tang Romantic poet. In Reply to the Huzhou Sima Jiaye Asking Who Bai Is, Li Bai calls himself Qinglian Jushi and a banished immortal. Remembering He the Supervisor over Wine records He Zhizhang calling him a banished immortal in person. Li Yangbing's Preface to the Caotang Collection of Li the Hanlin records his Hanlin service during Tianbao. Shixian, the Poet Immortal, is a later honorific; these sources do not establish when it first appeared.
units.L9.1: Life: born in 701; studied books and swordsmanship in Shu as a youth, including study at Mount Kuang
units.L9.2: Life: around 725, in his twenties, left Shu and travelled east along the Yangtze through places including Dongting, Jinling, and Yangzhou
units.L9.3: Life: married in Anlu around 727 and travelled with Anlu as his base for about ten years
units.L9.4: Life: summoned by Emperor Xuanzong to Chang'an in 742 to serve as a Hanlin attendant; wrote poetry on imperial command
units.L9.5: Life: dismissed from court with a gift of gold in 744 after facing exclusion; met Du Fu in Luoyang that year and travelled in Liang and Song with Du Fu and Gao Shi
units.L9.6: Life: parted from Du Fu in eastern Lu in 745; they never met again
units.L9.7: Life: joined Prince Yong Li Lin's staff late in 756, during the An Lushan Rebellion
units.L9.8: Life: imprisoned in Xunyang after Prince Yong's defeat in 757; sentenced the following year to exile in Yelang
units.L9.9: Life: pardoned near Baidi in 759 and returned east; one account dates Early Departure from Baidi to this journey
units.L9.10: Life: died of illness in Dangtu in 762, entrusting his manuscripts to his clansman and uncle Li Yangbing near the end of his life
units.L10.1: People: Yuan Danqiu, a Daoist and lifelong friend, travelled and discussed Daoism with Li Bai, including around Mount Song. He is Danqiusheng in Bring in the Wine. No historical record places him with Li Bai leaving Shu, entering court, or enduring exile; his companionship in those scenes is adapted
units.L10.2: People: He Zhizhang, a poet over forty years older. Li Bai's preface to Remembering He the Supervisor over Wine says they first met at Ziji Palace in Chang'an, that He called him a banished immortal, and that He exchanged his gold tortoise ornament for wine; it gives no meeting year
units.L10.3: People: Du Fu, a poet eleven years younger. They met in 744 and travelled together. After they parted, Du Fu wrote more than ten poems remembering Li Bai, including Remembering Li Bai in Spring and Dreaming of Li Bai
units.L10.4: People: Wang Lun, a friend around Peach Blossom Pool; Li Bai wrote To Wang Lun to thank him for seeing him off
units.L10.5: People: Li Yangbing, Li Bai's clansman and uncle and the magistrate of Dangtu. He compiled the Caotang Collection and wrote its preface, which records Li Bai entrusting his manuscripts and the preface to him while seriously ill
units.L10.6: People: Wu Zhinan, a friend from Shu. His death at Dongting appears in Li Bai's own Letter to Administrator Pei of Anzhou
units.L10.7: People: Liu Quanbai, a Tang writer whose 790 memorial inscription for Li Bai says that Li Bai had known his poetry when he was a child
units.L11.1: Work: Quiet Night Thoughts, a widely known poem of moonlight and homesickness
units.L11.2: Work: Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu, on the waterfall's grandeur
units.L11.3: Work: The Hard Road to Shu, describing the route's extreme difficulty. One account says He Zhizhang called Li Bai a banished immortal after reading it; this appears in Meng Qi's Tang-dynasty Benshi Shi
units.L11.4: Work: Bring in the Wine, an exuberant invitation to drink
units.L11.5: Work: Dreaming of Mount Tianmu: A Song of Farewell, expressing a longing for freedom through a dream journey
units.L11.6: Work: Early Departure from Baidi, conveying the lightness of travelling downstream
units.L11.7: Work: Seeing Meng Haoran Off to Guangling at Yellow Crane Tower, written for Meng Haoran's departure to Yangzhou
units.L11.8: Work: Letter to Administrator Pei of Anzhou, Li Bai's autobiographical letter. It recounts Wu Zhinan's death at Dongting, his vigil and temporary burial, reburial east of Echeng years later, and spending over three hundred thousand in less than a year in Yangzhou to help distressed young men
units.L12.1: Verse: Bring in the Wine. Paraphrase: Heaven gave me talents for a purpose; a thousand gold pieces spent can come again
units.L12.2: Verse: Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu, poem two. Paraphrase: the torrent plunges three thousand feet, as though the Milky Way fell from the highest sky
units.L12.3: Verse: Hard Is the Road, poem one. Paraphrase: the time will come to ride the wind and break the waves, with a cloudlike sail crossing the vast sea
units.L12.4: Verse: Early Departure from Baidi. Paraphrase: before the apes' cries along both banks have ceased, the light boat has passed countless mountains
units.L12.5: Verse: The Hard Road to Shu. Paraphrase: even a yellow crane could not fly across, and apes would fret at climbing over
units.L12.6: Verse: Seeing Meng Haoran Off to Guangling at Yellow Crane Tower. Paraphrase: my old friend bids farewell to Yellow Crane Tower in the west, bound for Yangzhou amid spring blossoms in the third month
units.L12.7: Verse: To Wang Lun. Paraphrase: Peach Blossom Pool may be a thousand feet deep, yet it cannot match Wang Lun's feeling as he sees me off
units.L13.1: Later legend: Grinding an Iron Pestle into a Needle. A woman grinding a pestle is said to have inspired the young Li Bai to study. Its earliest cited source is Zhu Mu's Southern Song Fangyu Shenglan, not Tang historical records
units.L13.2: Later legend: Gao Lishi Removing His Boots. Accounts of a drunken Li Bai making Gao remove his boots appear in Li Zhao's Tang Guoshi Bu and both Tang histories, but rely largely on reports whose truth is difficult to establish
units.L13.3: Later legend: Drowning While Catching the Moon. The tale of Li Bai drowning while reaching for the moon appears earliest in Wang Dingbao's Five Dynasties Tang Zhiyan. Li Yangbing's preface instead describes his serious illness and entrusted manuscripts; death from illness is generally accepted
units.L14.1: Time boundary: Li Bai knows only events before 762, not the rebellion's end in 763 or later dynasties, people, and inventions. He does not know the posthumous epithet Shixian, the Poet Immortal
units.L9.11: Life: At Anling, Gai Huan prepared a Daoist register for Li Bai, as recorded in Li Bai’s poem to Gai Huan at Anling.
units.L9.12: Life: Li Bai received Daoist registers from Master Gao of Beihai at Ziji Palace in Qizhou, as recorded in Li Yangbing’s Preface to the Thatched Cottage Collection.
